stimulus.text:
“I long to hear that you have declared an independency — and by the way in the new Code of Laws which I suppose it will be necessary for you to make I desire you would Remember the Ladies, and be more generous and favourable to them than your ancestors. Do not put such unlimited power into the hands of the Husbands. Remember all Men would be tyrants if they could. If perticuliar care and attention is not paid to the Laidies we are determined to foment a Rebelion, and will not hold ourselves bound by any Laws in which we have no voice, or Representation.”
— Abigail Adams to John Adams, Braintree, March 31, 1776 (abridged; spelling as in the original)
stimulus.source_note: Abigail Adams to John Adams, March 31, 1776. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus viewed before writing — Abigail Adams to John Adams, March 31, 1776, public domain.

books.section: Topic 3.6 The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals, B. Evolving Ideas on Gender

stem: Adams's warning that women “will not hold ourselves bound by any Laws in which we have no voice, or Representation” most directly borrows the argument of

options.text: Patriots who said Parliament could not tax colonies without a voice in Parliament
Loyalists who said only Parliament could make laws for the American colonies
options.misconception: Loyalists defended Parliament's authority; Adams borrows the Patriots' argument against it, not the Loyalists' defense of it.

options.text: Enslaved people who petitioned for freedom in Massachusetts courts
options.misconception: Enslaved petitioners used the same language too, but Adams borrows the Patriots' tax argument itself, not a court case.

options.text: French revolutionaries who said all men are born free and equal
options.misconception: The French Declaration came in 1789, thirteen years after this letter; Adams borrows a Patriot argument from her own time.

rationales.A: Her words echo the Patriots' own claim: no laws, and no taxes, without representation. She turns the Revolution's argument about Parliament back on the men writing the new laws.
rationales.B: Loyalists stood for Parliament's power over the colonies; Adams uses the Patriots' case against that power.
rationales.C: Black petitioners did borrow this language, but the sentence echoes the Patriots' stand against Parliament, which came first.
rationales.D: 1789 is too late: the letter is from 1776, so she cannot be borrowing from the French Revolution.
rationales.general:
1. Hear the echo. “No voice, or Representation” repeats the Patriots' case against Parliament.
2. Ask who she aims it at. Not Parliament, but the men writing the new American laws.
3. Check the dates. Background: the French Declaration is 1789, too late to borrow from in 1776.
Remember: when a writer borrows a slogan, ask whose slogan it was first — and who it is now aimed at.
